name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,144

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Observer piece from reporter in major trouble

indicators.note: a piece taken from a word is a single letter of it, here the opening one
a thing placed in something else sits inside it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: major means large or important
the opening letter of the word
trouble as a noun, a nuisance or fuss

explanation.surface: A newspaper columnist for The Observer writes about some serious difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Observer' looks like the Sunday paper, but it is the definition: the all-seeing watcher of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four. The R slips inside BOTHER after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's dictator is the figure whose surveillance watches every citizen, hence the slogan that he is watching you.

clue.text: Detective writer born in Fife

blocks.note: first meaning: the Yorkshire inspector Alan in Peter Robinson's crime novels
second meaning: Iain, the Scottish novelist born in Dunfermline, author of The Wasp Factory

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one crime novelist, but the detective and the Fife-born writer are separate people sharing a surname. Fife is a county in eastern Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Robinson's inspector and the author of The Wasp Factory share one surname, so each sense yields the same word.

clue.text: Where one prepares to read my amusing novel

indicators.note: something novel is new, so the letters take on a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone settles down to read a funny book they have written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book to read, but it signals the rearrangement. To read a subject, in British usage, is to study it at university.
explanation.definitionFit: In Germany and much of Europe this is the academic secondary school that prepares pupils for university study.

clue.text: Pen new best-seller or write only occasionally

indicators.note: something made new is remade, so these letters are put in a different order
taking a word only now and then means keeping every other letter

blocks.note: taken as written, without the hyphen
taken as written
the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Advice to an author: dash off a fresh hit, or else hardly write at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a command to write; it is a noun for a writer. Robert Noonan wrote The Ragged-Trousered Philanthropists under this pen name, and the book became a classic only after his death.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen can stand for the person wielding it, a writer, and this was the pseudonym of a Hastings house painter turned novelist.

clue.text: A hack’s article about Macbeth’s Glamis?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps itself round the others

blocks.note: the definite article
taken as written
a hack is a worn-out horse, as is a nag

explanation.surface: A journalist writes a piece about Macbeth's castle at Glamis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' looks like a journalist, but it is an old horse. The question mark flags that Glamis is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth is hailed as Thane of Glamis, and the land a thane holds is called by this word, so Glamis is one.

clue.text: Drug son and composer of Lulu with bit of Junk in port

indicators.note: a bit of a word is just one letter of it, the leading one here
putting something in another word lodges it inside that word

blocks.note: E is short for ecstasy
S is the abbreviation for son
Alban Berg wrote the opera Lulu
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A drug-dealing son and an opera composer bring a cargo of junk into harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The J goes inside the composer's name, just after its first letter. Junk tempts as a Chinese ship in a port, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Esbjerg is a major North Sea harbour town on the west coast of Denmark's Jutland peninsula.

clue.text: Wharton would make one with her final cut

indicators.text: would make one with her final
indicators.note: the novelist's name equals the answer plus one more letter, so that letter has been removed

blocks.note: Edith Wharton, the American novelist, with her last letter dropped

explanation.surface: Edith Wharton would be satisfied with the final version of her text.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it backwards: the answer, joined with the final letter of 'her', would make Wharton's first name, Edith.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text or film is to trim and shorten it, so a cut and an edit are the same act.

clue.text: Hope initially to return and take in hit play

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the letters run the other way
to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: the Australian poet A. D. Hope, by his initials
to ram is to strike hard

explanation.surface: Someone hoping at first to go back and catch a successful show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope initially' looks like the letter H, but Hope is the poet Alec Derwent Hope and his initials are used. 'Hit play' looks like a success; 'play' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama is a work written for performance on stage, which is exactly what a play is.

clue.text: She dug the ground for Moortown’s farmer

indicators.note: something ground is crushed and broken up, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman did the digging on a farm at a place called Moortown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like the earth being dug, but it is the anagram signal. The poet farmed in Devon and his collection Moortown records that life.
explanation.definitionFit: The Poet Laureate kept a cattle farm called Moortown in Devon and wrote a sequence of poems about working it.

clue.text: Key study for one opinionated novel

blocks.note: A is a musical key
a study is a room for working in
to be for someone is to be with them, on their side
a means one
opinionated describes someone holding a firm view

explanation.surface: A crucial piece of research for a dogmatic work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key study' looks like an important piece of research, but key is a musical note and study is a room. Someone opinionated is a person with a view.
explanation.definitionFit: This is E. M. Forster's 1908 book about Lucy Honeychurch in Florence, later filmed by Merchant Ivory.

clue.text: Country gent backing island Zola’s first to leave!

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction
the first of a word is its opening letter alone
a letter that leaves is no longer there, so it is taken out

blocks.note: a gent is a man
the Spanish island in the Balearics
the opening letter of the novelist's name

explanation.surface: A country gentleman supports an island while Zola is the first to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country gent' looks like one phrase, a rural squire, but 'Country' is the definition. Ibiza loses its Z.
explanation.definitionFit: Namibia is a nation in south-west Africa, independent from South Africa since 1990, with Windhoek as its capital.

clue.text: English service held by one poet for another

indicators.note: something held by another thing is gripped inside it

blocks.note: a bard is a poet
E is the abbreviation for English
the Royal Navy, one of the armed services

explanation.surface: An English church service is taken by one poet standing in for another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' looks like a church service, but it is one of the armed forces. 'Another' is the definition, another poet, such as Oliver Bernard or Bernard of Cluny.
explanation.definitionFit: Several poets bear the name, among them the medieval monk Bernard of Cluny and the twentieth-century translator Oliver Bernard.

clue.text: New satire’s biting about Diderot’s form of wit

definitions.note: the answer names the form; it is used as a modifier in the phrase staircase wit

indicators.note: making something new means remaking it, so the letters take a fresh order
biting means gripping in the teeth, so one piece holds another in its jaws

blocks.note: the word with its S, taken as written
CA is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A new satirical piece cuts into Diderot's particular brand of humour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the Latin abbreviation circa here, not a container signal. Diderot described thinking of the perfect retort only on the stairs going out.
explanation.definitionFit: Diderot's esprit de l'escalier, or staircase wit, is the clever riposte that occurs to you only after leaving.

clue.text: Rota Kundera shows obsessive Japanese geeks

indicators.note: to show something is to display it, so the letters are on view in the words before

blocks.note: found inside the two words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: A duty roster from the novelist Milan Kundera reveals some Japanese fanatics.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the end of 'Rota' and the start of 'Kundera'. Kundera is the Czech novelist who wrote The Unbearable Lightness of Being.
explanation.definitionFit: In Japanese the term describes young people consumed by a hobby, typically anime, manga or computer games.

clue.text: Sort to hang around with a Dean of St. Patrick’s

indicators.note: hanging around something means staying on all sides of it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: to sort through things is to sift them
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A type of person who likes to loiter in the company of a Dublin cathedral dean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' looks like a noun, a kind of person, but it is the verb meaning to sift.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift, the satirist of Gulliver's Travels, served as Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin from 1713.

clue.text: Not one to criticize Coward plays with half-done scenes

indicators.note: something only half done stops midway, so the back half of the word is dropped
to play with something is to toy with it, so the letters are moved about

blocks.note: Noël Coward, the playwright, taken as written
the front three letters of the six

explanation.surface: A critic declines to attack Noël Coward's plays, even with scenes left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coward plays' looks like a playwright's works, but plays is the anagram signal. Coward is Noël Coward, the English playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treated as beyond criticism is one, like the animals revered in Hinduism that no one may harm.

clue.text: She penned an Irish castle‘s border at cost

blocks.note: a border is an edge
what a thing costs is its worth

explanation.surface: A woman sketched an Irish castle's boundary at some expense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An Irish castle' sounds like a building she drew, but it is her novel Castle Rackrent.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Edgeworth wrote Castle Rackrent in 1800, a satire on Anglo-Irish landlords often called the first regional novel.

clue.text: In a way, Pound had shown up Liberal author

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another
in a down entry, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a road is a way
L is the abbreviation for Liberal
L is the symbol for a pound sterling, from Latin libra
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ezra Pound had, in a sense, embarrassed a liberal writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like the poet Ezra Pound, but it is the currency. 'In a way' looks like 'somewhat', but the Liberal goes in a road.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh-born writer of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and Tales of the Unexpected is a famous storyteller.

clue.text: Play about an unknown band that’s bagged gong

blocks.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
y is an unknown quantity in algebra
a gong is slang for a medal or honour, such as the MBE
a band can be a line or stripe

explanation.surface: A stage show about an obscure group of musicians who have won an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'gong' look like music and percussion, but a gong is an honour, here the MBE (Member of the Order of the British Empire), and the band has bagged it just ahead of itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's late romance tells of the ancient British king and his wronged daughter Imogen.

clue.text: Rabid socialist dumps first two right-leaning characters?

indicators.note: dumping the opening pair means the front two letters are thrown away
rabid means wild and frenzied, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the word without its opening pair of letters

explanation.surface: A fanatical left-winger drops two leading right-wingers from the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right-leaning characters' sounds like conservative people, set up by 'socialist', but it means letters that slope to the right.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic type slants rightwards, so its letters lean to the right; the question mark flags the pun on politics.

clue.text: A complex, creative work church member cut up

indicators.note: something cut is cut short, so it loses its final letter
in a down entry, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: art is creative work
CE is the Church of England
a member is a limb, a leg, here without its last letter

explanation.surface: A complicated, imaginative piece of work that a churchgoer tore apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A complex' looks like the start of a description; it is a definition, one psychological complex. 'Member' looks like a congregant, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Jung named a daughter's rivalry with her mother after the Greek heroine, as the counterpart to Freud's Oedipus complex.

clue.text: Greek mistress melts after one replaces wife

indicators.note: one thing replacing another takes its place, so a letter is swapped out

blocks.note: to melt is to thaw
the Roman numeral for one
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A Greek lover softens once another woman supplants a man's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One replaces wife' sounds like adultery, which suits a mistress, but it swaps a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Thaïs was a famous Athenian courtesan who accompanied Alexander the Great on his campaigns, later an opera by Massenet.

clue.text: Old work about Stoppard’s West End shows

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters are reversed
an across entry reads west to east, so a word's west end is its leading letter

blocks.note: ex means former
op is short for opus, a work
the opening letter of the playwright's name

explanation.surface: An early play concerns Tom Stoppard's theatre productions in London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End shows' looks like London theatre, but the West End is the left end of a word. Stoppard is the English playwright Tom Stoppard.
explanation.definitionFit: Expos are exhibitions, large trade fairs or displays, so they are shows in the sense of public exhibitions.

clue.text: Charge raised by one’s Italian love rival

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters means they read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a rap is a criminal charge, as in a murder rap
the Roman numeral for one
the S of the possessive, taken as written

explanation.surface: An accusation is brought by someone's Italian romantic competitor.
explanation.walkthrough: Count Paris is the suitor Juliet's parents want her to marry in Romeo and Juliet, set in Verona.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's tragedy the young nobleman seeks Juliet's hand, making him Romeo's rival in Verona.

clue.text: Ludwig Van fan having beer with Queen around ten

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the earlier pieces encircle the next one

blocks.note: ale is a beer
and means together with
Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A Beethoven devotee drinks beer with the monarch at about ten o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten goes in just after the beer. 'Ludwig Van' is how Alex, narrator of A Clockwork Orange, refers to Beethoven, whom he adores.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgess's teenage thug Alex, a Beethoven lover, is often taken to be short for the full first name given here.

clue.text: Girl to have a drink with? Tea, perhaps!

definitions.text: Girl to have a drink with?

blocks.clueFragment: Girl to have a drink with?
blocks.note: first meaning: the girl in the title of Laurie Lee's Cotswold memoir, paired with cider
second meaning: Cockney rhyming slang for tea, short for a name rhyming with it

explanation.walkthrough: The drink is cider, from Laurie Lee's memoir of a Cotswold childhood. Rosie Lee is Cockney rhyming slang for tea, and Lee links the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: The memoir title pairs the girl with cider, while London rhyming slang shortens 'Rosie Lee' to mean a cuppa.

clue.text: Army musician alit without case on Central Line

indicators.note: a word stripped of its case has lost its outer letters at each end

blocks.note: the core is the central part
L is the abbreviation for line
the word minus its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A military bandsman got off the Tube without his instrument case on the Central Line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central Line' looks like the London Underground line but splits into two pieces. Captain Corelli is the mandolin-playing Italian officer in Louis de Bernières's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Antonio Corelli, an Italian soldier occupying Cephalonia, plays the mandolin in de Bernières's Captain Corelli's Mandolin.

clue.text: Take back covers publisher filled with atomic reptiles

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters are turned round
to cover something is to go over and around it, so one piece encloses another
a thing filled with something holds it inside, so a piece goes within

blocks.note: to take an exam is to sit it
A as in A-bomb, the atomic bomb
Pan Books, the paperback publisher

explanation.surface: A publisher is told to retract its book covers, which are full of nuclear lizards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take back' looks like retract, but 'Take' means sit, as in sitting an exam. A-bomb gives the atomic A.
explanation.definitionFit: Taipans are highly venomous Australian snakes, and snakes are reptiles, so these are examples of the class.

clue.text: “Come, come, you –; i’faith, you are angry” (Taming of the Shrew)

definitions.text: “Come, come, you –; i’faith, you are angry” (Taming of the Shrew)

blocks.clueFragment: “Come, come, you –; i’faith, you are angry”
blocks.note: the quotation with one word removed
the source: Petruchio's wooing of Katherina in Act 2 of Shakespeare's comedy

explanation.walkthrough: The blank is the insect Petruchio calls Katherina in their first sparring match; she replies that if she is one, he should beware her sting.
explanation.definitionFit: Petruchio likens the shrewish Katherina to a stinging insect, an apt image for her sharp, angry tongue.

clue.text: Ladies crow about man with conviction for love?

indicators.note: about can mean in a disordered state, all around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Women gloat over a man who sincerely believes in romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conviction' looks like strong belief, but it is a court conviction: the writer was jailed in 1895 for gross indecency, for 'the love that dare not speak its name'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish playwright was convicted and imprisoned for his homosexual relationships, so his love brought him a criminal conviction.
